task.title: Flow text into columns
task.shortdesc: A multi-column element flows its content down a first column, then down the next one, and so on, as a newspaper does. You choose the number of columns or their width, the space between them and a line to draw there. The columns reference lists the properties used here.

image.alt: A box with a heading across its whole width. Under it, three columns of lines of text, with a vertical rule in the gap between the first and the second column and between the second and the third.

context.p: The element names in the examples, such as article, are placeholders. Use the names that occur in your XML.

step.cmd: Choose the number or the width of the columns

info.p: Set column-count on a block element to divide its content into that number of columns:

Set column-width instead to give the least width of a column. The element gets as many columns of that width as fit, and the columns are widened to fill the element. When you give both, column-count is the most columns that you get. The shorthand columns sets both: columns: 3 and columns: 12em are valid.
A multi-column element is a new formatting context. A float before it does not reach into its columns: the element stands beside the float, narrower, and its columns share the width that is left.

step.cmd: Set the gap and the rule

info.p: column-gap is the space between two columns. Its initial value, normal, is 1em. column-rule draws a line in the middle of each gap, with the width, the style and the color of a border:
A rule is drawn only between two columns that have content.

step.cmd: Place the columns in the width of the element

info.p: With column-width, the columns are widened to fill the element. Set justify-content to keep them at the width you give and to choose where the space that is left goes:

ul.li: normal, the initial value, and stretch widen the columns.
start, center and end keep the columns together at the start, in the middle or at the end of the element. left and right put them on that side of the lines.
space-between puts the first column at the start and the last one at the end, and shares the space between the columns.
space-around gives each column the same space on both sides, so the two ends get half as much as each gap.
space-evenly makes the space at each end and between the columns the same.

fig.title: The values of justify-content on columns

image.alt: Seven elements with three columns each. With normal the columns fill the element. With start, center and end the columns keep their width and stand together at the start, in the middle or at the end. With space-between the first and the last column touch the ends and the gaps are wider. With space-around the ends get half the space of each gap, and with space-evenly they get the same space.

info.p: The space put between the columns widens the gaps, and a rule stays in the middle of its gap. With column-count alone, the columns always fill the element.

align-content places the columns in the height of an element that is taller than they are, as it places the content of any box. The columns of an element with a height are as tall as the element, so align-content moves them when the element ends with an element that spans the columns, or when it has a min-height and no height. Box sizes lists its values.

step.cmd: Balance the columns or fill them one by one

info.p: By default, the columns of an element are as even as they can be, so the text is shared in equal parts. column-fill: auto fills each column up to the height of the element, or to the bottom of the page when the element has no height, before it starts the next column:

The columns of an element with a height are as tall as the element, and so are the rules between them. When the content is short, balanced columns share it evenly at the top of the element. When it is too long for the height, the columns are filled one by one.

Set break-before: column on a block inside the multi-column element to start it at the top of the next column, or break-after: column to start the next block there. Inside columns, always is a column break too:

Balanced columns stay as short as they can around a column break. A column break before the first block of the element changes nothing: it stays in the columns, and the element stays where it is. A page break before that block goes to the element, which then starts on a new page.

step.cmd: Let a heading go across the columns

info.p: A block element inside the multi-column element can have column-span: all. It is as wide as the element, and the content before it and the content after it are laid out in columns of their own. The columns before it are as even as they can be, whatever column-fill says:

When the content is longer than the page, the columns go on to the next page. Each page has its own columns, and the text reads in order through all of them. On every page but the last, the columns go down to the bottom of the page. On the last page they are balanced, unless you set column-fill: auto.

The columns follow the writing mode. In vertical lines, the columns are one above the other, and the lines of each column are as long as a column is tall. A vertical element inside horizontal text takes the height you give it; without one, CSSMedia sizes it and sets a long text in columns by itself, balanced unless you set column-fill: auto. explains writing modes and boxes of another writing mode.

result.p: The content of your element flows into columns.
